ela_passages.title: The Playful Side of Bumblebees
ela_passages.modeled_on: Exam A — The Best Laid Plans of Ravens

paragraphs.text: In cartoons and picture books, bees are often shown laughing, dancing, and playing games as if they were tiny people. Playful bees may seem to be nothing more than the wild imaginings of artists, but a study published in the journal Animal Behaviour hints that one particular idea behind those cartoons might not be as far-fetched as it seems. For most of human history, people assumed that insects do not experience the world in the same way people do. Some people believed that insects might learn simple lessons, such as where to find flowers, and that instinct might drive them to work tirelessly for their colonies, but most people did not think that insects had the ability to play. At Queen Mary University of London, researchers argue that bumblebees may play, choosing to do certain activities simply because they enjoy them.

It can be difficult to test whether an animal is playing because human observers must be certain they are not mistaking useful behavior for play. For example, bees spend much of their day flying from flower to flower and crawling over blossoms, but scientists who study animals would not call this play. This activity is simply a matter of survival. Animal behavior scientists argue that in order for an activity to count as play, it must have no obvious purpose, such as getting food, and the animal must choose to do it again and again while it is calm and not under threat.

To avoid mistaking useful behavior for evidence of play, the Queen Mary researchers designed two experiments to test whether bumblebees play. Bumblebees are close relatives of honeybees, insects known for remarkable behavior such as the “waggle dance” that honeybees use to tell their nestmates where to find food. A study in 2017 by scientists at the same university showed that bumblebees could learn to roll a ball into a goal to earn a sugary reward, which suggests that bees can handle objects in surprisingly flexible ways. In order to find out whether bees would handle objects even when there was no reward, the researchers had to design experiments in which ball rolling could not be explained by a search for food. Therefore, the bees were given objects that they never encounter in the wild: small balls.

For the first experiment, the researchers built an arena with a clear path leading from the bees’ nest to a feeding area stocked with sugar water. Once the bees had learned the route, the researchers placed small balls in areas to the side of the path. Even though the balls offered no food, many bees went out of their way to push and roll them, and some came back to roll them again and again. Over the course of the experiment, the bees traveled back and forth through the arena many times. The second experiment involved two rooms of different colors. One room always held balls, and the other room never did. Later, the researchers removed all the balls and let the bees choose between the two empty rooms. The bees more often chose the room with the color that had once held the balls, even though the balls were gone. The researchers also noticed that younger bees rolled balls more often than older bees did, a pattern seen in many animals, whose young tend to play more than adults.

The results of these experiments are exciting, but more evidence needs to be gathered before scientists can fully conclude that bumblebees play. Some scientists argue that the bees might have been rolling the balls simply to explore unfamiliar objects, not necessarily because they enjoyed it. Regardless, like other recent advances in animal science, these experiments show that bumblebees could be much more complex than first believed, and some scientists now believe that insects may experience something like enjoyment.

questions.question:
Read this sentence from paragraph 1.

**At Queen Mary University of London, researchers argue that bumblebees may play, choosing to do certain activities simply because they enjoy them.**

Which sentence from paragraph 4 provides support for this argument?

options.A: “The bees more often chose the room with the color that had once held the balls, even though the balls were gone.”
options.B: “Once the bees had learned the route, the researchers placed small balls in areas to the side of the path.”
options.C: “One room always held balls, and the other room never did.”
options.D: “Later, the researchers removed all the balls and let the bees choose between the two empty rooms.”

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks which sentence from paragraph 4 supports the argument in paragraph 1 that bumblebees may play because they enjoy it.

A is CORRECT. This is the only option that describes a choice the bees made. Even after the balls were removed, the bees went back to the room that reminded them of the balls. That suggests the bees remembered ball rolling as something pleasant and wanted more of it, which is exactly what “enjoy” means.

B is wrong. It only tells what the researchers did (put balls beside the path). It says nothing about how the bees reacted.

C is wrong. It describes how the researchers set up the rooms, not anything the bees did.

D is wrong. It describes the researchers removing the balls and setting up the test, but stops before telling us what the bees chose.

Coaching tip: when a question asks for evidence about an animal’s ability, look for the sentence where the animal acts or chooses, not the sentences where the scientists set things up.

questions.modeled_on_question: Exam A — The Best Laid Plans of Ravens — AR08

questions.question:
Read these sentences from paragraph 2.

**For example, bees spend much of their day flying from flower to flower and crawling over blossoms, but scientists who study animals would not call this play. This activity is simply a matter of survival.**

Which statement describes the effect of the phrase “simply a matter of survival” in the passage?

options.A: It implies that bees are skilled at finding the flowers that contain the most food.
options.B: It emphasizes that bees visit flowers because they need food, not because they enjoy it.
options.C: It conveys that bees will usually prioritize gathering food over other activities.
options.D: It suggests that bees often gather more food than their colony will be able to use.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks what the phrase “simply a matter of survival” does in paragraph 2.

B is CORRECT. The paragraph is explaining the difference between useful behavior and play. Calling flower visits “simply a matter of survival” tells the reader that bees do this because they must eat to stay alive, so it does not count as play. The last sentence of paragraph 2 backs this up: to count as play, an activity “must have no obvious purpose, such as getting food.”

A is wrong. The passage never discusses how skilled bees are at picking the best flowers.

C is wrong. The phrase is not about which activity bees put first. It is about why they visit flowers (for food, not fun).

D is wrong. Nothing in the passage says bees collect more food than they need.

Coaching tip: the word “simply” is a clue. It shrinks the activity down to one plain purpose, which is staying alive.

questions.modeled_on_question: Exam A — The Best Laid Plans of Ravens — AR09

questions.question: In the first experiment described in paragraph 4, which of the bees’ behaviors provides the strongest evidence for the claim that bumblebees play?

options.A: They drank sugar water at the feeding area.
options.B: They traveled back and forth through the arena many times.
options.C: They learned the route from the nest to the feeding area.
options.D: They went out of their way to roll balls that offered no food.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks which behavior in the first experiment best shows that bumblebees play.

D is CORRECT. Paragraph 2 says that for something to count as play, it must have no obvious purpose, such as getting food, and the animal must choose to do it again and again. Paragraph 4 says that “even though the balls offered no food, many bees went out of their way to push and roll them, and some came back to roll them again and again.” That matches the definition of play exactly.

A is wrong. Drinking sugar water is eating. It has an obvious purpose, so it is the opposite of play.

B is wrong. The bees traveled through the arena to reach the food, so these trips are explained by hunger, not fun. This is related to the experiment but is not strong evidence of play.

C is wrong. Learning the route shows that bees can learn, but learning how to get to food is not play.

Coaching tip: go back to paragraph 2’s definition of play and check each option against it.

questions.modeled_on_question: Exam A — The Best Laid Plans of Ravens — AR10

questions.question: How does paragraph 5 fit into the overall structure of the passage and contribute to the development of ideas?

options.A: It introduces a problem with the results of the Queen Mary study, suggesting that some scientists believe that further research will not lead to a clear answer.
options.B: It provides a conclusion to the information about the Queen Mary study, indicating that some scientists think further research is needed in order to prove the idea.
options.C: It lists the effects of the Queen Mary study, implying that researchers should have designed experiments that better separated play from exploring.
options.D: It summarizes the final steps of the Queen Mary study, emphasizing the difficulties researchers had in telling the difference between play and exploring.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks what job paragraph 5 does in the passage.

B is CORRECT. Paragraph 5 is the conclusion. It says the results are “exciting” but that “more evidence needs to be gathered before scientists can fully conclude that bumblebees play,” and it mentions that some scientists think the bees might just have been exploring. It ends by saying the experiments show bees “could be much more complex than first believed.” That is a wrap-up that calls for more research.

A is wrong. The paragraph says more evidence is needed, not that more research will fail to give a clear answer.

C is wrong. The paragraph does not list effects of the study, and the author never criticizes how the experiments were designed.

D is wrong. Paragraph 5 does not describe any steps of the experiments; those are in paragraph 4.

Coaching tip: a last paragraph that calls results exciting but asks for more evidence is a conclusion with a caution, not a criticism.

questions.modeled_on_question: Exam A — The Best Laid Plans of Ravens — AR11

questions.question: The author conveys a point of view on the study of animal behavior **mainly** by

options.A: explaining how modern experiments show that earlier beliefs about insects are inaccurate.
options.B: comparing the results of different experiments that were designed to test animal intelligence.
options.C: critiquing experiments that aimed to show that certain insects are capable of play.
options.D: sharing details about experiments that tested whether an animal is capable of play.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks how the author mainly gets their point of view across.

D is CORRECT. Most of the passage (paragraphs 3 and 4) walks through the details of the two experiments: the arena, the balls, the colored rooms, and what the bees did. The author shows a positive view by calling the results “exciting” and saying they show bees “could be much more complex than first believed” (paragraph 5).

A is wrong. Paragraph 1 mentions old beliefs about insects, but the author does not say those beliefs have been proven wrong. The passage only says bees “could be” more complex and that “more evidence needs to be gathered.” This option goes too far.

B is wrong. The two experiments are presented as working together to test the same idea. The author never compares their results against each other.

C is wrong. The author admits more evidence is needed but does not criticize the experiments.

Coaching tip: ask “what does the author spend the most words on?” Here it is the details of the experiments.

questions.modeled_on_question: Exam A — The Best Laid Plans of Ravens — AR12

questions.question: With which statement would the author of the passage **most likely** agree?

options.A: Scientists should be careful about drawing conclusions from experiments that give animals unfamiliar objects.
options.B: Scientists can confirm whether insects play by performing experiments on other insects known for complex behavior, such as honeybees.
options.C: Scientists should continue researching to determine whether insects can experience something like enjoyment.
options.D: Scientists are unlikely to be able to design an experiment that can truly tell the difference between play and exploring in insects.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks which statement fits the author’s views best.

C is CORRECT. Paragraph 5 says that “more evidence needs to be gathered before scientists can fully conclude that bumblebees play,” and that some scientists now believe insects “may experience something like enjoyment.” The author is excited about the results but wants more research, which is exactly what C says.

A is wrong. Paragraph 5 does mention that the bees might have been exploring unfamiliar objects, but the author does not warn against this kind of experiment. Instead the author says the experiments show bees “could be much more complex than first believed.”

B is wrong. Honeybees are mentioned in paragraph 3 only to show that bees are known for remarkable behavior. The passage never suggests testing other species.

D is wrong. The author never suggests that a good experiment is impossible. Calling the results “exciting” shows the author thinks this research is worth continuing.

Coaching tip: watch out for options that take a word from the passage (like “honeybees” or “unfamiliar objects”) and turn it into an idea the author never states.

questions.modeled_on_question: Exam A — The Best Laid Plans of Ravens — AR13

ela_passages.title: Running Against the Rules
ela_passages.modeled_on: Exam A — Champion of the Channel

paragraphs.text: In 1966 the director of the Boston Marathon sent a letter to Roberta “Bobbi” Gibb, a young woman who had been training on long runs for about two years, turning down her application to enter the race. He explained that women were not physiologically able to run a marathon and that, under the rules of the time, women were not allowed to compete in races of that length. Yet, at twenty-three years old, Gibb not only became the first woman to run the entire Boston Marathon, she also finished ahead of about two-thirds of the men in the race. Bobbi Gibb’s run from Hopkinton to Boston was a testimony to her determination, resourceful spirit, and love of running.

Running a marathon is a daunting task for any athlete. The Boston course stretches twenty-six miles and 385 yards, from the small town of Hopkinton to the heart of Boston. After many miles of rolling roads, runners must climb a series of hills in the city of Newton, the last of which is known as Heartbreak Hill, just when their legs are most tired. Blisters, cramps, and dehydration present added hazards, and many runners “hit the wall” late in the race, when the body runs low on stored energy.

For decades the marathon was considered far too grueling for women. Since the first Boston Marathon in 1897, only men had been allowed to enter. Gibb, too, had been turned away: the race director’s letter made it clear that she could not run as an official entrant. Undeterred, Gibb decided to run anyway, without an official race number. Gibb knew that if race officials spotted her at the starting line, they might pull her out of the race before she had the chance to prove what a woman could do.

To prepare for the race, Gibb found ways to work around the obstacles in her path. Running shoes made for women were almost impossible to find, so she bought a pair of boys’ running shoes. During her training she had worn nurses’ shoes, which were designed for walking hospital hallways rather than for running and which, over long miles on hard roads, offered little cushioning or support, making an already punishing task almost unbearable. Gibb also planned a disguise: she would wear her brother’s Bermuda shorts and a baggy hooded sweatshirt over a black swimsuit. Unlike a typical woman’s athletic outfit, this one would help her blend in with the men on the starting line.

On the morning of April 19, 1966, Gibb hid in a clump of forsythia bushes near the starting line in Hopkinton. When the starting gun fired, she waited until about half of the runners had passed, then slipped into the crowd. At first her heart pounded, and she worried that someone would recognize her and order her off the course. Under the heavy sweatshirt, she grew uncomfortably hot. Soon, though, the men running around her realized that she was a woman. Instead of reporting her, they told her that they would not let anyone throw her out of the race. Relieved, Gibb pulled off her sweatshirt and ran openly, settling into a steady, comfortable pace.

Throughout Gibb’s run, the people around her cheered her on. The men running near her chatted with her and encouraged her. As word spread, radio reporters announced that a woman was running in the marathon, and spectators along the route began watching for her. When she passed Wellesley College, a school for women, the students cheered wildly.

For miles Gibb ran happily, enjoying the cheers of the crowds that lined the road. However, when she reached the hills of Newton, the race became a struggle. Her new running shoes, which she had not had time to break in, rubbed painful blisters on her feet, and her legs grew heavy and stiff. Yet Gibb felt a rising excitement as she pushed on, sensing that she was about to prove the doubters wrong. Finally, she reached the top of the last hill. With the hardest part of the course behind her, she headed downhill toward the city and the finish line.

After three hours, twenty-one minutes, and forty seconds, Gibb, on aching feet, crossed the finish line in Boston. The crowd cheered, reporters rushed to interview her, and the governor of Massachusetts, John Volpe, stepped forward to shake her hand. Gibb had run into history.

In the days that followed, newspapers carried the story of the woman who had run the Boston Marathon. Not only were many people amazed by Gibb’s run, but it also helped change what they believed women could do. Gibb returned to run the race again in 1967 and 1968, and in 1972 the Boston Marathon officially opened its starting line to women. Bobbi Gibb’s run proved to the world that with determination and resourcefulness, it was possible for a person to achieve his or her goals.

ela_passages.passage_figure_html:
MILESTONES FOR WOMEN IN MARATHON RUNNING
YearMilestone
1966Bobbi Gibb becomes the first woman to run the entire Boston Marathon (without a race number).
1967Kathrine Switzer becomes the first woman to run the Boston Marathon wearing an official race number.
1972The Boston Marathon officially opens to women. Nina Kuscsik is the first official women’s winner.
1984The first women’s Olympic marathon is held. Joan Benoit of the United States wins the gold medal.

questions.question: What do the race director’s comments in paragraph 1 reveal about the challenges Gibb faced in attempting her run?

options.A: In spite of her training, Gibb faced social as well as physical obstacles in attempting to run the marathon.
options.B: Regardless of her ability, Gibb was at a serious disadvantage compared with local runners who were more familiar with the Boston course.
options.C: At the time, Gibb still needed more training in order to succeed at running such a long distance.
options.D: While Gibb could take part in shorter races, some people were uncomfortable with her attempt because no woman had ever tried it before.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks what the race director’s comments in paragraph 1 show about Gibb’s challenges.

A is CORRECT. The director said women “were not physiologically able to run a marathon” and that the rules did not allow women to race that far. That shows a social obstacle (people in charge did not believe in women and would not let them in) on top of the physical obstacle of running more than twenty-six miles. Paragraph 1 also tells us she had been “training on long runs for about two years,” so the doubts came from her being a woman, not from a lack of preparation.

B is wrong. The director’s comments have nothing to do with knowing the course or where Gibb lived.

C is wrong. The passage says she had trained for about two years. The director did not say she needed more training. He said women in general could not do it.

D is wrong. The director’s point was that women’s bodies could not handle a marathon, not that people felt uneasy because it had never been tried.

Coaching tip: “social” means obstacles coming from other people and society’s rules, while “physical” means obstacles from the body and the course.

questions.modeled_on_question: Exam A — Champion of the Channel — AR20

questions.question:
Read this sentence from paragraph 4.

**During her training she had worn nurses’ shoes, which were designed for walking hospital hallways rather than for running and which, over long miles on hard roads, offered little cushioning or support, making an already punishing task almost unbearable.**

The word “unbearable” is used to highlight

options.A: that Gibb’s running shoes needed to be custom made for her race.
options.B: that the flaws in Gibb’s training shoes made a difficult task even harder.
options.C: how Gibb came up with a creative way to blend in with the other runners.
options.D: how the nurses’ shoes made it impossible for Gibb to train for long distances.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks why the author uses the word “unbearable,” which means “too painful or difficult to put up with.”

B is CORRECT. The sentence says long-distance running was “already punishing” and that the nurses’ shoes, with “little cushioning or support,” made it “almost unbearable.” The word stresses that the bad shoes made a hard job even harder.

A is wrong. Nothing in the passage says her shoes had to be custom made. In fact, she bought ordinary boys’ running shoes.

C is wrong. Gibb’s disguise is described later in paragraph 4, but the word “unbearable” is about the shoes, not about blending in.

D is wrong. The sentence says “almost” unbearable, not impossible, and paragraph 1 says Gibb had been “training on long runs for about two years.” The shoes made training painful, but they did not stop her.

Coaching tip: notice the little word “almost.” It keeps the meaning at “extremely hard,” not “impossible.”

questions.modeled_on_question: Exam A — Champion of the Channel — AR21

questions.question: Which statement describes how the author’s use of a problem-and-solution structure in paragraph 5 contributes to the development of ideas in the passage?

options.A: Detailing how hot Gibb became under her sweatshirt highlights the effectiveness of her disguise.
options.B: Explaining the difficulties that arose early in the race helps predict the additional obstacles that occurred later in Gibb’s run.
options.C: Showing how Gibb went from hiding in fear to running openly reveals that the marathon was an emotional as well as a physical challenge.
options.D: Describing Gibb’s worries at the start of the race provides evidence of the careful planning required to keep her hidden.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks how the problem-and-solution pattern in paragraph 5 adds to the passage.

C is CORRECT. The problem: at the start, Gibb’s “heart pounded,” she “worried that someone would recognize her,” and she was hot under the sweatshirt. The solution: the men around her said they would not let anyone throw her out, so, “relieved,” she took off the sweatshirt and “ran openly.” Moving from fear to relief shows that the race tested her feelings and nerve, not just her legs.

A is wrong. Being too hot was a drawback of the disguise. The paragraph does not use it to show that the disguise worked well.

B is wrong. The early problems (fear and heat) are not used to predict the later problems (hills and blisters in paragraph 7). They are different kinds of problems.

D is wrong. Her worries show how she felt, not how much planning it took. Her planning is described in paragraph 4.

Coaching tip: for a problem-and-solution question, name the problem and the solution out loud first, then ask what that change shows about the person.

questions.modeled_on_question: Exam A — Champion of the Channel — AR22

questions.question: Which sentence best supports the idea that Gibb succeeded in running the marathon because of her resourceful approach to the challenge?

options.A: “The men running near her chatted with her and encouraged her.” (paragraph 6)
options.B: “At first her heart pounded, and she worried that someone would recognize her and order her off the course.” (paragraph 5)
options.C: “Yet, at twenty-three years old, Gibb not only became the first woman to run the entire Boston Marathon, she also finished ahead of about two-thirds of the men in the race.” (paragraph 1)
options.D: “When the starting gun fired, she waited until about half of the runners had passed, then slipped into the crowd.” (paragraph 5)

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks which sentence best shows that Gibb’s clever, resourceful thinking helped her succeed.

D is CORRECT. Gibb could not enter the race officially, so she came up with a plan: hide in the bushes, wait until about half the runners passed, then slip into the crowd where officials would not notice her. That clever plan is what got her onto the course at all.

A is wrong. The other runners’ encouragement helped Gibb, but it was their kindness, not her own resourceful approach.

B is wrong. This sentence describes her fear. It shows how she felt, not a clever method she used.

C is wrong. This sentence shows that her run was historic, but it does not say how she managed to do it.

Coaching tip: “resourceful” means finding a smart way around a problem. Look for the sentence where Gibb herself solves a problem.

questions.modeled_on_question: Exam A — Champion of the Channel — AR23

questions.question: Paragraph 7 contributes to the development of a central idea of the passage by

options.A: emphasizing the excitement Gibb felt, despite her pain, as she came closer to achieving her goal.
options.B: illustrating that Gibb’s physical strength and mental toughness allowed her to stay focused on her goal.
options.C: conveying that Gibb pushed herself to the edge of her physical capabilities in order to finish the race.
options.D: highlighting the impact the steep hills had on Gibb’s emotions during the race.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks how paragraph 7 helps develop a central idea of the passage.

A is CORRECT. Paragraph 7 is full of Gibb’s feelings. She “ran happily, enjoying the cheers,” and even when blisters and heavy legs slowed her down, she “felt a rising excitement as she pushed on, sensing that she was about to prove the doubters wrong.” This builds the central idea that her love of running and determination carried her through.

B is wrong. The paragraph does not say that strength and toughness kept her focused. It focuses on her emotions.

C is wrong. The paragraph does mention blisters and heavy legs, but it does not say she reached the limit of what her body could do. This option also leaves out the paragraph’s main focus, her feelings.

D is wrong. The hills made the race physically harder, but her excitement came from getting closer to proving the doubters wrong, not from the hills.

Coaching tip: when a paragraph mixes hardship and feelings, check which one the author keeps coming back to. Here the hardship is the background and the feelings are the point.

questions.modeled_on_question: Exam A — Champion of the Channel — AR24

questions.question: Which sentence from the passage best conveys the author’s perspective regarding the impact of Gibb’s accomplishment?

options.A: “Gibb had run into history.” (paragraph 8)
options.B: “Undeterred, Gibb decided to run anyway, without an official race number.” (paragraph 3)
options.C: “Yet Gibb felt a rising excitement as she pushed on, sensing that she was about to prove the doubters wrong.” (paragraph 7)
options.D: “For miles Gibb ran happily, enjoying the cheers of the crowds that lined the road.” (paragraph 7)

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks which sentence shows what the author thinks about how important Gibb’s run was.

A is CORRECT. “Gibb had run into history” is the author’s own judgment that the run was a historic event with a lasting impact.

B is wrong. This sentence shows Gibb’s determination, but it tells what Gibb decided, not what the author thinks about the run’s impact.

C is wrong. This sentence also describes Gibb’s own feelings in the moment, not the author’s view of the run’s impact.

D is wrong. This sentence describes how Gibb felt during the race. It does not give the author’s opinion of the run’s importance.

Coaching tip: “author’s perspective” means the writer’s opinion. Look for a sentence where the writer steps back and judges the event, rather than describing what the person did or felt.

questions.modeled_on_question: Exam A — Champion of the Channel — AR25

questions.question: Which sentence is the best summary of the steps that Gibb took to prepare for the Boston Marathon?

options.A: Gibb hid in a clump of bushes near the starting line and slipped into the crowd after about half of the runners had passed.
options.B: Gibb focused on finding better shoes than the nurses’ shoes that had made her training so difficult.
options.C: Gibb replaced the nurses’ shoes she had trained in with a pair of boys’ running shoes and planned a disguise of her brother’s Bermuda shorts and a hooded sweatshirt so that she could blend in with the men at the start.
options.D: Gibb ran alongside men who promised that they would not let anyone throw her out of the race.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks for the best summary of how Gibb prepared before race day.

C is CORRECT. Gibb’s preparation is described in paragraph 4. This option covers both of her main steps: getting better shoes (boys’ running shoes instead of nurses’ shoes) and planning a disguise (her brother’s Bermuda shorts and a hooded sweatshirt) to blend in.

A is wrong. Hiding in the bushes and slipping into the crowd happened on race morning (paragraph 5). Those are actions during the race, not preparation.

B is wrong. Getting better shoes was only one of her steps. This option leaves out the disguise, so it is not a complete summary.

D is wrong. The men’s promise happened during the race (paragraph 5), and it was something other people did, not one of Gibb’s preparation steps.

Coaching tip: a good summary covers all of the main points of the section, not just one, and stays within that section.

questions.modeled_on_question: Exam A — Champion of the Channel — AR26

questions.question: The idea that many people were interested in Gibb’s run is illustrated in the passage **mainly** through the

options.A: information about the race director’s letter turning down Gibb’s application.
options.B: information about the men who ran beside Gibb and encouraged her during the race.
options.C: details about how Gibb’s run helped change what people believed women could do.
options.D: details about the radio reports of Gibb’s progress during the race and the reaction when she finished.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks how the passage mainly shows that many people were interested in Gibb’s run.

D is CORRECT. Paragraph 6 says that “radio reporters announced that a woman was running in the marathon, and spectators along the route began watching for her.” Paragraph 8 says that at the finish “the crowd cheered, reporters rushed to interview her,” and the governor shook her hand. Paragraph 9 adds that newspapers carried her story. All of these show wide public interest.

A is wrong. The letter shows that one official did not want her in the race. It does not show that many people were interested.

B is wrong. The men near her were only a small group of fellow runners, not the wider public.

C is wrong. Changing people’s minds was an effect that came after the race. It does not show the public’s interest while she was running.

Coaching tip: “many people” means the public, such as crowds, reporters, and newspapers, not just the few people right next to her.

questions.modeled_on_question: Exam A — Champion of the Channel — AR27

questions.question: How does the table mainly build on information presented in the passage?

options.A: It allows for a comparison of the finishing times of women marathon runners, building on the idea that Gibb finished ahead of about two-thirds of the men.
options.B: It shows that women continued to gain official places in marathon running after 1966, building on the idea that Gibb’s run helped change what people believed women could do.
options.C: It shows that the later women listed were inspired to run by Gibb, building on the idea that her run changed people’s minds.
options.D: It shows that Gibb returned to run the Boston Marathon in later years, building on the idea that she remained determined after her first race.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks how the table adds to the passage.

B is CORRECT. The table shows women moving from running without a number (1966) to wearing an official number (1967), to being officially welcomed at Boston (1972), to having their own Olympic marathon (1984). This builds on paragraph 9’s idea that Gibb’s run “helped change what [people] believed women could do.”

A is wrong. The table contains no finishing times at all, so it cannot be used to compare times.

C is wrong. The table lists what each woman did but never says that Gibb inspired them. That would be reading something into the table that it does not show.

D is wrong. Paragraph 9 says Gibb ran again in 1967 and 1968, but the table lists only her 1966 run. The table does not show her later races.

Coaching tip: for a table question, check every option against what is actually printed in the table. Wrong answers often mention something true from the passage that the table does not show.

ela_passages.title: The City That Lit the World
ela_passages.modeled_on: Exam A — Massachusetts: Lowell National Historical Park

paragraphs.text: During the first half of the 19th century, New Bedford, Massachusetts, quickly transformed itself from a small seaport into the whaling capital of the world. In time, New Bedford gained worldwide recognition for its huge fleet of whaling ships, its busy wharves and workshops, its grand houses, and the whale oil that lit lamps in homes and streets across America and Europe. Young farm boys, sailors from distant islands, and curious travelers all flocked to New Bedford to sign on to a whaling voyage or to see the bustling port for themselves. As the writer Herman Melville, who sailed on a whaling voyage from the New Bedford area as a young man, observed in his novel Moby-Dick, the town’s fine houses and flowery gardens “came from the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian oceans. One and all, they were harpooned and dragged up hither from the bottom of the sea.” Today, New Bedford Whaling National Historical Park welcomes visitors to explore the city’s historic streets and learn about the history of the port that once led the world in whaling.

When New Bedford became a town in 1787, Quaker merchants, including members of the Rotch family from nearby Nantucket Island, had already begun basing whaling ships along the Acushnet River to take advantage of its deep, sheltered harbor. Unlike Nantucket’s harbor, which was partly blocked by a sandbar, New Bedford’s harbor could easily hold the large, heavy ships that long whaling voyages required. Wharves lined with warehouses, candle factories, rope-making sheds, and shipyards stretched along the waterfront, where tall-masted ships crowded the harbor. The most recognized of the park’s historic sites are the Seamen’s Bethel, a sailors’ chapel dedicated in 1832; the Rotch-Jones-Duff House, a whaling merchant’s mansion built in 1834; the U.S. Custom House, completed in 1836; and the New Bedford Whaling Museum, founded in the early 1900s. By the 1850s, hundreds of whaling ships called New Bedford home, and its whaling fleet was the largest in the world.

The men who crewed New Bedford’s whaling ships were significant in the history of the city. In the early 1800s, many young men left the quiet, predictable routine of New England farm life for adventure at sea. Most were young, single “greenhands,” sailors with no experience, who were tired of the limited opportunities offered by farm work. Young men found that whaling ships offered them a share of a voyage’s profits, called a “lay,” along with food and a bunk. Although these men gained the chance to see the world, the ship’s captain and officers controlled nearly every part of their lives, and voyages commonly lasted three or four years. Aboard ship, sailors were expected to follow strict orders, standing watch day and night and obeying the captain without question.

Yankee greenhands continued to fill most whaling crews until the middle of the 1800s, when a growing nation began to offer young men other ways to earn a living in factories, on railroads, and out West. As whales near home grew scarce, voyages stretched longer, yet pay for ordinary sailors stayed low. These low wages, harsh conditions, and years away from home led many sailors to quit after a single voyage, and some deserted their ships in faraway ports, especially during the California Gold Rush of 1849. When conditions did not improve, the Yankee sailors left whaling behind, and island sailors from the Azores and Cape Verde, where whaling ships often stopped for supplies, replaced them in the crews. Despite the low pay and dangerous work, these islanders were eager to find work.

The sailors replacing the Yankee greenhands during the middle and late 1800s were predominantly Portuguese-speaking islanders from the Azores and Cape Verde, many of whom left home to escape poverty and, in Cape Verde, repeated droughts. Although New Bedford’s ships took on a growing number of islanders during this time, sailors of many backgrounds had been part of the city’s whaling history from its beginning, and African American and Wampanoag men had served aboard whaling ships since the industry’s earliest days, some rising to become officers and even captains. Initially, many people in New Bedford were slow to welcome the Portuguese-speaking newcomers, who faced prejudice because of their language, their religion, and, for many Cape Verdeans, the color of their skin. Islanders made up a large share of whaling crews until the industry faded, and many of them settled in New Bedford with their families.

Like the Yankee greenhands before them, the island sailors who crewed New Bedford’s ships faced long voyages, low pay, and dangerous work. By the time whaling declined, New Bedford had become a meeting place of many cultures, where Portuguese-speaking families built churches, clubs, and neighborhoods of their own, and where Cape Verdean traditions still thrive today. The whaling industry declined steadily after oil was discovered in Pennsylvania in 1859, because kerosene, a fuel made from petroleum, was cheaper than whale oil and soon replaced it in lamps across the country. Despite a brief boom in demand for baleen, the flexible material from the mouths of some whales that was used in products such as corsets and buggy whips, the last whaling voyages from New Bedford came to an end in the 1920s.

questions.question:
Read this sentence from paragraph 1.

**As the writer Herman Melville, who sailed on a whaling voyage from the New Bedford area as a young man, observed in his novel Moby-Dick, the town’s fine houses and flowery gardens “came from the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian oceans. One and all, they were harpooned and dragged up hither from the bottom of the sea.”**

The author **most likely** includes the quotation from Melville in order to

options.A: convey the idea that New Bedford’s wealth and beauty came from the whaling industry.
options.B: suggest that people around the world admired the homes and gardens of New Bedford.
options.C: compare the wealth of New Bedford with the wealth of other American cities.
options.D: imply that whalers brought plants and building materials home from distant oceans.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks why the author included Melville’s words in paragraph 1.

A is CORRECT. Melville is speaking figuratively. When he says the houses and gardens were “harpooned and dragged up … from the bottom of the sea,” he means they were paid for with money from hunting whales in faraway oceans. The quotation shows that the city’s beauty and wealth came from whaling.

B is wrong. The quotation is the opinion of one writer. It does not tell us what people around the world thought, and it is about where the wealth came from, not about admiring it.

C is wrong. The quoted words do not mention any other city, so there is no comparison.

D is wrong. This reads the quotation too literally. Whalers did not actually haul up houses or gardens from the sea. Melville means the money to build them came from whaling.

Coaching tip: when a quotation sounds impossible if you take it literally, ask what it means figuratively.

questions.modeled_on_question: Exam A — Massachusetts: Lowell National Historical Park — AR36

questions.question: Which description from the passage **best** conveys the central idea that New Bedford was “the port that once led the world in whaling” (paragraph 1)?

options.A: the reference to the farm boys, island sailors, and travelers who flocked to New Bedford
options.B: the details about the growth of New Bedford’s whaling fleet and the people who worked on its ships throughout the city’s history
options.C: the reference to the African American and Wampanoag sailors who served aboard whaling ships from the industry’s earliest days
options.D: the details about the young Yankee men and the island sailors who worked aboard New Bedford’s ships

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks which part of the passage best shows that New Bedford led the world in whaling.

B is CORRECT. The whole passage builds this idea. Paragraph 2 describes the harbor, the waterfront, the historic buildings, and the fact that by the 1850s New Bedford’s “whaling fleet was the largest in the world.” Paragraphs 3–6 then follow the different groups of sailors who worked on its ships over time. Together, the fleet’s growth and its workforce show how important the port was.

A is wrong. The people who flocked to the city (paragraph 1) show the port was popular, but this one detail is not enough to show it led the world in whaling.

C is wrong. This is one detail from paragraph 5. It is important, but by itself it does not show that New Bedford led the world.

D is wrong. The sailors are an important part of the passage, but this option leaves out the growth of the fleet and the port, which is what made New Bedford a world leader.

Coaching tip: a central idea is usually supported by details across the whole passage, so the best answer is often the broadest one that is still accurate.

questions.modeled_on_question: Exam A — Massachusetts: Lowell National Historical Park — AR37

questions.question: Which sentence from paragraph 2 **best** supports the idea that New Bedford became “the whaling capital of the world” (paragraph 1) in a short period of time?

options.A: “When New Bedford became a town in 1787, Quaker merchants, including members of the Rotch family from nearby Nantucket Island, had already begun basing whaling ships along the Acushnet River to take advantage of its deep, sheltered harbor.”
options.B: “Wharves lined with warehouses, candle factories, rope-making sheds, and shipyards stretched along the waterfront, where tall-masted ships crowded the harbor.”
options.C: “By the 1850s, hundreds of whaling ships called New Bedford home, and its whaling fleet was the largest in the world.”
options.D: “The most recognized of the park’s historic sites are the Seamen’s Bethel, a sailors’ chapel dedicated in 1832; the Rotch-Jones-Duff House, a whaling merchant’s mansion built in 1834; the U.S. Custom House, completed in 1836; and the New Bedford Whaling Museum, founded in the early 1900s.”

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks which sentence in paragraph 2 best shows that New Bedford became the world’s whaling capital quickly.

C is CORRECT. This sentence gives both parts of the idea: a time (“by the 1850s”) and the result (“the largest in the world”). New Bedford only became a town in 1787, so reaching the world’s largest fleet within about one lifetime shows fast growth.

A is wrong. This sentence tells when the town began and why the harbor was a good spot, but it says nothing about how big the whaling business became or how fast.

B is wrong. This sentence shows that the waterfront was busy, but it gives no time frame, so it does not show the growth happened quickly.

D is wrong. This sentence lists historic buildings, and its dates stretch from 1832 to the early 1900s, which does not show quick growth. It also does not show that New Bedford led the world.

Coaching tip: the question has two parts (“whaling capital” and “short period of time”). The right answer has to support both.

questions.modeled_on_question: Exam A — Massachusetts: Lowell National Historical Park — AR38

questions.question:
Read this sentence from paragraph 3.

**In the early 1800s, many young men left the quiet, predictable routine of New England farm life for adventure at sea.**

Which statement **best** describes how the sentence fits into the overall structure of the passage?

options.A: It indicates a shift in tone from positive and hopeful to negative and dissatisfied with life aboard whaling ships.
options.B: It summarizes a challenge that led many young men to leave their farms and seek work at sea.
options.C: It begins a comparison of whaling crews between the early 1800s and the late 1800s.
options.D: It provides a transition from a description of the city and its waterfront to a description of the men who worked aboard its ships.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks what job this sentence does in the structure of the whole passage.

D is CORRECT. Paragraphs 1 and 2 describe the city, the harbor, and the waterfront. This sentence turns the passage toward the people who worked on the ships, and the rest of paragraph 3 and all of paragraph 4 go on to describe those young sailors.

A is wrong. The sailors’ unhappiness comes later, in paragraph 4 (“These low wages, harsh conditions, and years away from home led many sailors to quit”). This sentence itself is hopeful (“adventure at sea”), so it does not mark a shift to a negative tone.

B is wrong. The sentence does mention the “quiet, predictable routine” of farm life, but its main job is to move the passage to a new topic, not to sum up a challenge.

C is wrong. The sentence introduces the young Yankee sailors. It does not set up a comparison between crews of different time periods.

Coaching tip: “how does this sentence fit the overall structure” questions are usually about what comes before and after. Check the paragraphs on both sides.

questions.modeled_on_question: Exam A — Massachusetts: Lowell National Historical Park — AR39

questions.question:
Read this sentence from paragraph 5.

**Although New Bedford’s ships took on a growing number of islanders during this time, sailors of many backgrounds had been part of the city’s whaling history from its beginning, and African American and Wampanoag men had served aboard whaling ships since the industry’s earliest days, some rising to become officers and even captains.**

How does this sentence contribute to the development of ideas in the passage?

options.A: It emphasizes the important role that sailors of many backgrounds played in New Bedford’s whaling history.
options.B: It implies that New Bedford was founded by African American and Wampanoag sailors.
options.C: It highlights the working relationship between the Yankee greenhands and the island sailors.
options.D: It suggests that the island sailors were readily accepted into the community.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks what this sentence adds to the passage.

A is CORRECT. The sentence points out that New Bedford’s whaling crews were diverse from the very beginning, and that African American and Wampanoag men served on whaling ships and some became officers and captains. This stresses that many different groups helped build the city’s whaling history.

B is wrong. The sentence says these men served on whaling ships, not that they founded the town. Paragraph 2 says Quaker merchants were basing ships there when the town began.

C is wrong. The sentence does not mention the Yankee greenhands at all, and the passage never describes how they worked together with the islanders.

D is wrong. The very next sentence says the opposite: people in New Bedford “were slow to welcome the Portuguese-speaking newcomers, who faced prejudice.”

Coaching tip: use the sentences right around the quoted sentence to rule out choices that the passage contradicts, like D.

questions.modeled_on_question: Exam A — Massachusetts: Lowell National Historical Park — AR40

questions.question: Which sentence **best** summarizes the young Yankee sailors’ experience as the main workforce on New Bedford’s whaling ships?

options.A: At first the young men were satisfied with whaling, but as they left the ships, islanders arrived to fill the empty places.
options.B: Young men eagerly went to sea in search of adventure, but when low pay and harsh conditions did not improve, they left whaling for other opportunities.
options.C: Young men left home to go whaling, but they soon became unhappy with the long voyages and strict discipline aboard ship.
options.D: The young men were eager to leave farm life behind, so they signed on to whaling ships in New Bedford.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks for the best summary of what happened to the young Yankee sailors (paragraphs 3 and 4).

B is CORRECT. It covers the whole story: the young men eagerly left farms “for adventure at sea” (paragraph 3), conditions such as “low wages, harsh conditions, and years away from home” wore them down, and “when conditions did not improve, the Yankee sailors left whaling behind” for other work (paragraph 4).

A is wrong. It says they left and were replaced but never explains why they left, which is a key part of paragraph 4.

C is wrong. It includes their unhappiness but leaves out what they did about it. They quit, deserted, and finally left whaling, which is how their time as the main workforce ended.

D is wrong. It covers only the beginning of the story, why they joined. It leaves out what happened to them and why they left.

Coaching tip: a strong summary has a beginning, middle, and end. Check that the answer includes all three.

questions.modeled_on_question: Exam A — Massachusetts: Lowell National Historical Park — AR41

questions.question: The reason New Bedford lost its status as the world’s whaling capital is **best** illustrated through the

options.A: explanation of why the island sailors faced prejudice in New Bedford.
options.B: information about the brief boom in demand for baleen.
options.C: description of the long voyages, low pay, and dangerous work aboard whaling ships.
options.D: comparison between whale oil and a cheaper fuel made from petroleum.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks which part of the passage best explains why New Bedford stopped being the whaling capital.

D is CORRECT. Paragraph 6 says the whaling industry “declined steadily after oil was discovered in Pennsylvania in 1859, because kerosene, a fuel made from petroleum, was cheaper than whale oil and soon replaced it in lamps across the country.” Once people could buy a cheaper fuel, the demand for whale oil dropped.

A is wrong. Prejudice against the islanders (paragraph 5) is part of the city’s history, but the passage does not connect it to the end of whaling.

B is wrong. The baleen boom was a short exception that kept some whaling going for a while. It did not cause the decline.

C is wrong. The hard conditions explain why the Yankee sailors left (paragraph 4), but the ships kept sailing with island crews. The passage never says these conditions ended the industry.

Coaching tip: look for signal words like “because” that state a cause directly.

ela_passages.title: The Benefits of Walking Breaks
ela_passages.modeled_on: Exam A — The Benefits of Indoor Plants

sentence_paragraphs.text: In an age of video games, streaming shows, and online homework, it is easy to see why people spend so much of the day sitting down.
According to studies that track people’s daily movements, many American adults spend more than half of their waking hours sitting.
Doctors say that this lack of movement puts people at risk for physical and psychological problems.
Whenever people stand up and walk, their working muscles use sugar from the blood for energy, and their hearts beat faster, which helps keep the heart strong.
Sitting for hours at a time, without breaks, deprives people of these benefits.
Too little movement over many years can raise a person’s risk of heart disease.
This link first came to light in the 1950s, when a British researcher noticed that the conductors on London’s double-decker buses had fewer heart attacks than the drivers.
Researchers determined the key difference to be physical activity.
The drivers sat behind the wheel for their entire shifts, while the conductors climbed up and down the buses’ stairs all day to collect fares.
More recent studies have found a simple way to reduce the harm of long hours in a chair: break them up with short walks.
Taking walking breaks has psychological benefits too.
Research has long linked physical activity with better moods and lower levels of stress.
While a long workout at the gym is an excellent way to improve a person’s mental health, recent research has indicated that even a short walk can also help.
To experience the greatest benefit, experts suggest standing up and moving around for at least a few minutes every hour.
Moving more often, even if it is just a quick walk down the hallway, is a significant factor in a person’s well-being.
Many schools have also cut back on recess, and students need more time to play team sports like soccer and basketball.
Many doctors put it simply: the human body was built to move, and it works best when people give it the chance.

questions.question: Which sentence should follow sentence 3 to **best** introduce the topic of the passage?

options.A: People who sit for most of the day can develop heart disease, weight gain, and higher levels of stress.
options.B: It is important for people to realize that they need to be more active, whether through sports, exercise classes, or daily walks.
options.C: Taking short walking breaks throughout the day can be a simple way to undo some of the harm of too much sitting.
options.D: For their health, people need to join a gym or take regular breaks from sitting.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks which sentence would best introduce what the whole passage is about.

C is CORRECT. The passage is about one specific solution: short walking breaks. The second paragraph (sentences 4–10) explains the physical benefits, and the third paragraph (sentences 11–14) explains the mental benefits. This sentence names that topic and connects it to the problem of too much sitting from sentences 1–3.

A is wrong. It just repeats the problem from sentence 3 (risks of too much sitting). It does not introduce the solution the passage is about.

B is wrong. It is too broad. The passage is not about sports or exercise classes. It focuses on short walking breaks.

D is wrong. It offers two different solutions (joining a gym or taking breaks). The passage is about breaks, and sentence 13 even says a short walk can help, not just a long gym workout.

Coaching tip: an introduction sentence should point to what the rest of the passage actually discusses, not more and not less.

questions.modeled_on_question: Exam A — The Benefits of Indoor Plants — AR43

questions.question: Which transition word or phrase should be added to the beginning of sentence 5 to emphasize the relationship between sentences 4 and 5?

options.A: In addition,
options.B: Unfortunately,
options.C: As a result,
options.D: Primarily,

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks which transition best shows how sentence 5 connects to sentence 4.

Sentence 4 describes something good: walking helps muscles use blood sugar and keeps the heart strong. Sentence 5 says that sitting for hours “deprives people of these benefits.” The connection is good news followed by a regrettable loss.

B is CORRECT. “Unfortunately,” signals that what comes next is a disappointing or negative turn, which is exactly what sentence 5 is: people miss out on the benefits just described.

A is wrong. “In addition,” adds another point of the same kind. Sentence 5 is not another benefit. It is the loss of the benefits.

C is wrong. “As a result,” would mean sentence 5 is caused by sentence 4. But walking’s benefits do not cause people to sit for hours.

D is wrong. “Primarily,” means “mainly” and is used to point out the most important cause or item. Sentence 5 is not naming a main item.

Coaching tip: first say in plain words how the two sentences relate (here, “good thing, then losing it”), then pick the transition that matches.

questions.modeled_on_question: Exam A — The Benefits of Indoor Plants — AR44

questions.question: Which sentence could **best** follow sentence 13 to support the ideas in the third paragraph (sentences 11–14)?

options.A: In one study, office workers who took short walks during the workday reported feeling more energetic and less stressed than on days when they stayed at their desks.
options.B: A study found that a short walk after a meal can help the body control the amount of sugar in the blood.
options.C: A survey found that one shopping mall is popular with families because its long, wide hallways make it a pleasant place to stroll.
options.D: A recent study revealed that people who regularly play team sports tend to have more close friends, suggesting that sports help people build social connections.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks which sentence would best support the third paragraph, which is about the psychological (mental and emotional) benefits of walking breaks.

A is CORRECT. It gives research evidence that short walks during the day made people feel “more energetic and less stressed.” That is a mental benefit of short walks, which is exactly what sentence 13 claims (“even a short walk can also help”).

B is wrong. Controlling blood sugar is a physical benefit. It fits the second paragraph (sentences 4–10), not the third paragraph about mental health.

C is wrong. It is about why a mall is popular with families, not about how walking makes individual people feel.

D is wrong. It is about team sports and friendships, not about short walking breaks or mood. It drifts away from the paragraph’s point.

Coaching tip: first name the paragraph’s main idea (here, “walking breaks help your mind”), then pick the sentence that gives evidence for exactly that idea.

questions.modeled_on_question: Exam A — The Benefits of Indoor Plants — AR45

questions.question: Which sentence presents ideas irrelevant to the topic of the passage and should be deleted?

options.A: sentence 12
options.B: sentence 14
options.C: sentence 16
options.D: sentence 17

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks which sentence is off-topic and should be removed.

C is CORRECT. Sentence 16 (“Many schools have also cut back on recess, and students need more time to play team sports like soccer and basketball”) changes the subject to school recess and team sports. The passage is about short walking breaks during the day, so this sentence pulls the reader off track.

A is wrong. Sentence 12 (“Research has long linked physical activity with better moods and lower levels of stress.”) sets up the third paragraph’s point about mental benefits; the sentences after it connect that idea directly to short walks.

B is wrong. Sentence 14 gives a practical tip (move for a few minutes every hour) that directly supports the passage’s point about walking breaks.

D is wrong. Sentence 17 (“Many doctors put it simply: the human body was built to move, and it works best when people give it the chance.”) is the passage’s closing thought. It sums up the main idea that people should move more often, so it belongs.

Coaching tip: a sentence can sound related (it mentions being active) and still be off-topic. Ask, “Is this about the exact subject of the passage?”

questions.modeled_on_question: Exam A — The Benefits of Indoor Plants — AR46

questions.question: Which concluding sentence should follow sentence 17 to **best** support the information presented in the passage?

options.A: Experts say that a pedometer, a smartwatch, or a simple phone alarm can remind you to stand up and move around during the day.
options.B: As one famous study showed, bus conductors who climbed stairs all day had fewer heart attacks than the drivers who sat.
options.C: Because walking keeps the heart healthy, it is one of the best ways to lower the risk of heart disease.
options.D: More people should consider building short walking breaks into their days to improve their overall well-being and reverse some of the negative effects of a sit-down society.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks which sentence would make the best ending for the whole passage.

D is CORRECT. It ties together the passage’s main points: it recommends the solution (short walking breaks), mentions “overall well-being” (both the physical and mental benefits), and connects back to the problem from the first paragraph (“a sit-down society”).

A is wrong. It gives a small practical tip about reminders. That is a narrow detail, not a conclusion that sums up the passage.

B is wrong. It repeats one example from sentences 7–9. Repeating one detail does not wrap up the whole passage.

C is wrong. It only mentions the heart, which is the physical benefit from the second paragraph. It leaves out the mental benefits in the third and fourth paragraphs.

Coaching tip: a good conclusion covers all the big ideas of the passage. If an option only covers one paragraph, it is too narrow.
